mainEntity.name: How do you know when a wood fence needs to be replaced instead of repaired?

acceptedAnswer.text: Push on the posts, not the panels. If more than 30 percent of them move or are soft at the grass line when you probe with a screwdriver, replacement is cheaper than repairing. On a 176-foot fence at eight-foot bays, that is about seven posts out of 23. Below that threshold, section repair is genuinely the better spend, and a contractor who tells you otherwise is selling, not advising.

mainEntity.name: How much does it cost to remove an old fence in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Removal runs $3 to $7 per linear foot in 2026, or roughly $500 to $1,200 for a typical backyard fence, and that price usually assumes the footings stay in the ground. Concrete footings are a separate line item at $2 to $3 each to break out, plus disposal. On our Troy project, removal was $563 and footing breakout was another $506 for 23 posts.

mainEntity.name: Why do wood fences lean in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always because the footing is above frost depth. Michigan's residential code puts frost depth at 42 inches, and a footing at 22 inches sits inside the freeze zone, so it lifts a little every winter and settles back less each spring. Twenty-two cycles of that is a fence that has slowly pushed itself out of the ground, which is exactly what we found on this job.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a permit to replace a fence in Troy, Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Troy City Code Chapter 83, Section 5 requires a Building Department permit before any fence is constructed, and that includes a replacement on an existing line. The fee follows Chapter 60, Section 60.03. One catch: no permit issues until the lot's final grading is approved, and a fence in an easement also needs Public Works sign-off, so verify the grading history before scheduling demolition.

mainEntity.name: How tall can my fence be in Troy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Six feet above existing grade in residential districts under Chapter 83, Section 2(A), dropping to 30 inches for any portion in front of the front building setback line. Qualifying corner lots can run a 48-inch non-obscuring fence along the common street line. No fence over 30 inches may sit within the 25-foot sight triangle at an intersection. The Building Board of Appeals can waive height limits.

mainEntity.name: Can you install a fence in November in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes, until the ground freezes hard, often late November, sometimes early December if snow insulates the soil. Posts still have to reach 42 to 48 inches, and digging gets slower and more expensive as the season closes. This project ran in early November with no frost in the ground. Staining has to wait for spring regardless, because the finish will not cure below 50 degrees.

mainEntity.name: Can I reuse the old post holes and footings?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and it costs more to try. Old footings are usually wider at the base than the hole you need, and most were poured as bells that cannot be pulled, so they have to be broken out. Setting a new post beside an old footing means an oversized hole in disturbed soil, which is a worse foundation than a fresh one. Break them out and dig clean.

mainEntity.name: What do I do with the old pressure-treated boards?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treated lumber is construction and demolition debris, not yard waste. It does not go in curbside yard waste, it does not go in compost, and it must not be burned: Michigan's open-burning rules prohibit it because the preservative concentrates in the ash and goes into the air. Haul it to a licensed C&D disposal site. Sound cedar pickets can be salvaged for garden projects; treated pine should not be used for vegetable beds.
